whyNext: Builds on side-length extension from Maximal Square (Seq 259) by recognizing that if a cell is the bottom-right corner of a square of size k, it also forms squares of sizes 1 through k, so summing all dp[i][j] gives the total count.
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the side length of the largest square of all 1s whose bottom-right corner is at (i, j).
If matrix[i][j] == 1, dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]).
The value of dp[i][j] is precisely the number of squares with bottom-right corner at (i, j); sum all dp[i][j] across the grid.

brute.idea: For every cell (r, c), test all possible square side lengths k extending down and right, verifying all cells contain 1.
steps: Iterate over each top-left cell (r, c).
For each possible side length k: check if all elements in grid[r..r+k-1][c..c+k-1] are 1.
Increment total count if valid; break as soon as a 0 is found.
Return total count.
brute.whySlow: Checks O(m*n*min(m, n)) squares taking O(min(m, n)^2) per verification.

optimal.idea: Dynamic programming where dp[i][j] is the largest square ending at (i, j); summing dp[i][j] counts all squares in O(m * n) time.
steps: Initialize dp array of dimensions m x n (or reuse matrix).
For each cell (i, j): if matrix[i][j] == 1, if i == 0 or j == 0, dp[i][j] = 1, else dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]).
Add dp[i][j] to total answer.
Return total count.

whyNext: Builds on grid dynamic programming from Count Square Submatrices with All Ones (Seq 487) by tracking both maximum and minimum path products at each cell because multiplying by a negative cell can turn a minimum into a maximum.
hints: Any path from (0, 0) to (m-1, n-1) can only move right and down.
Because grid numbers can be negative, keep track of both the maximum product and the minimum product reachable at each cell (i, j).
If grid[i][j] is negative, the new maximum product comes from min(prev) * grid[i][j] and the new minimum comes from max(prev) * grid[i][j].

brute.idea: DFS traversal exploring all right and down paths to cell (m-1, n-1), computing the product along each path.
steps: Recursive function dfs(r, c, currentProduct).
If (r, c) == (m-1, n-1), update global maxProduct with currentProduct.
Branch to (r+1, c) and (r, c+1) if within grid bounds.
Return global maxProduct % 1_000_000_007 (or -1 if strictly negative).
brute.whySlow: Explores all C(m+n-2, m-1) grid paths exponentially.

optimal.idea: 2D dynamic programming maintaining maxDp[i][j] and minDp[i][j] in 64-bit integers to prevent overflow during calculations.
steps: Create maxDp and minDp of size m x n initialized with grid[0][0].
Fill first row and first column using products from adjacent cells.
For each cell (i, j): consider candidates from top (maxDp[i-1][j]*val, minDp[i-1][j]*val) and left (maxDp[i][j-1]*val, minDp[i][j-1]*val).
Set maxDp[i][j] to max candidate and minDp[i][j] to min candidate.
If maxDp[m-1][n-1] < 0 return -1; else return maxDp[m-1][n-1] % 1_000_000_007.

whyNext: Builds on 2D grid path counting from Unique Paths (Seq 254) by introducing boundary escape conditions and a maximum step budget, requiring 3D state dp[k][i][j] representing remaining moves.
hints: Let dp[k][r][c] be the number of paths that start at (r, c) and exit the boundary in at most k moves.
Base cases: when a move lands outside [0, m-1] x [0, n-1], it counts as 1 valid path out.
Transitions: sum ways to exit from the four neighbors with k-1 moves remaining, modulo 10^9+7.

brute.idea: Recursive DFS exploring up to maxMove steps in 4 cardinal directions, tallying moves that step out of grid bounds.
steps: Recursive dfs(r, c, movesLeft).
If r < 0 or r >= m or c < 0 or c >= n: return 1 (escaped).
If movesLeft == 0: return 0 (trapped).
Sum results from dfs on 4 adjacent cells with movesLeft - 1.

optimal.idea: Iterative dynamic programming updating a 2D matrix of reach counts across maxMove steps in O(maxMove * m * n) time.
steps: Initialize dp[m][n] with 0, and dp[startRow][startColumn] = 1.
For step 1 to maxMove: create nextDp[m][n] = 0.
For each cell (r, c) with dp[r][c] > 0, consider moving to all 4 neighbors.
If neighbor is out of bounds, add dp[r][c] to total paths out.
Otherwise, add dp[r][c] to nextDp[nr][nc].
Set dp = nextDp.
Return total % 1_000_000_007.

whyNext: Builds on multi-dimensional grid DP from Out of Boundary Paths (Seq 489) by coordinating two robots moving simultaneously row-by-row with state dp[r][c1][c2], avoiding double-counting when they land on the same cell.
hints: Both robots advance one row downward simultaneously at each step, so state only needs (row, col1, col2).
From state (r, c1, c2), each robot has 3 choices (-1, 0, +1), yielding 3 x 3 = 9 possible transitions for the next row.
If c1 == c2, cherries are collected only once: grid[r][c1]; otherwise: grid[r][c1] + grid[r][c2].

brute.idea: Recursively simulate all 9 simultaneous moves per row until reaching the bottom row.
steps: Recursive dfs(r, c1, c2).
If c1 or c2 is outside [0, cols-1], return invalid (-infinity).
Compute current cherries: grid[r][c1] + (c1 != c2 ? grid[r][c2] : 0).
If r == rows - 1, return current cherries.
Explore all combinations of dc1 in {-1, 0, 1} and dc2 in {-1, 0, 1} on r + 1.
Return cherries + max child result.

optimal.idea: 3D Dynamic Programming (or bottom-up 2D DP) storing maximum cherries for each (col1, col2) pair at each row in O(rows * cols^2) time.
steps: Initialize dp[n][n] table with -1, dp[0][n-1] = grid[0][0] + grid[0][n-1].
For row r from 1 to m-1: create nextDp initialized with -1.
For each reachable (c1, c2) in dp: iterate through all 9 move pairs (dc1, dc2) for nc1 = c1 + dc1, nc2 = c2 + dc2.
If nc1 and nc2 in bounds: gain = grid[r][nc1] + (nc1 != nc2 ? grid[r][nc2] : 0); nextDp[nc1][nc2] = max(nextDp[nc1][nc2], dp[c1][c2] + gain).
Set dp = nextDp.
Return maximum value in dp after processing all rows.

whyNext: Builds on 2D string comparison DP from Longest Common Subsequence (Seq 261) with the contiguous subarray requirement, resetting the DP cell to 0 whenever elements differ instead of taking max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
hints: Subarrays must be contiguous, so when nums1[i] != nums2[j], the repeated length resets to 0.
Let dp[i][j] be the length of the longest common suffix of prefixes nums1[0..i-1] and nums2[0..j-1].
If nums1[i-1] == nums2[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; track the overall maximum.

brute.idea: Compare all pairs of start indices (i, j) in nums1 and nums2, extending matching contiguous elements.
steps: Iterate i through all indices of nums1.
Iterate j through all indices of nums2.
While i + k < len(nums1) and j + k < len(nums2) and nums1[i+k] == nums2[j+k]: increment k.
Track the maximum k achieved.
Return maximum length.

optimal.idea: 2D dynamic programming storing matching suffix lengths in O(n * m) time and O(m) space.
steps: Create dp array of size m+1 where dp[j] holds matching suffix length ending at nums2[j-1].
Iterate i from 1 to n: iterate j from m down to 1.
If nums1[i-1] == nums2[j-1]: dp[j] = dp[j-1] + 1, maxLen = max(maxLen, dp[j]).
Else: dp[j] = 0.
Return maxLen.

whyNext: Builds on cost-weighted character alignment from Edit Distance (Seq 263) by replacing uniform edit costs with the ASCII code point values of deleted characters to find the minimum deletion cost to equalize two strings.
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the minimum ASCII deletion cost to make prefixes s1[0..i) and s2[0..j) equal.
Base cases: dp[i][0] is the sum of ASCII values in s1[0..i); dp[0][j] is the sum in s2[0..j).
If s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; else: min(dp[i-1][j] + ascii(s1[i-1]), dp[i][j-1] + ascii(s2[j-1])).

brute.idea: Recursively check matching characters from indices (i, j) and branch into deleting from s1 or deleting from s2.
steps: Recursive dfs(i, j):
If i == 0, return sum of ASCII values of s2[0..j).
If j == 0, return sum of ASCII values of s1[0..i).
If s1[i-1] == s2[j-1], return dfs(i-1, j-1).
Else return min(dfs(i-1, j) + s1[i-1], dfs(i, j-1) + s2[j-1]).

optimal.idea: 2D dynamic programming filling a cost table of size (n+1) x (m+1) in O(n * m) time and O(m) space.
steps: Initialize dp array of size m+1 where dp[j] is the delete cost for s2[0..j) against an empty s1.
Populate base case dp[j] = dp[j-1] + s2[j-1].
For each character s1[i-1]: update dp row using a prevDiag variable to hold dp[i-1][j-1].
If s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]: dp[j] = prevDiag; else: dp[j] = min(dp[j] + s1[i-1], dp[j-1] + s2[j-1]).
Return dp[m].

whyNext: Builds on palindromic DP from Longest Palindromic Subsequence (Seq 269) by recognizing that the minimum insertions required to make a string palindromic equals the string length minus the length of its longest palindromic subsequence.
hints: Any characters that already form the Longest Palindromic Subsequence (LPS) do not need counterpart insertions.
The minimum insertions needed is exactly n - LPS(s).
Compute LPS using 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the LPS length of substring s[i..j].

brute.idea: Recursively compare outer characters: if they match, shrink both ends; otherwise, try inserting a character to match either end and take the minimum insertions.
steps: Recursive helper dfs(i, j):
If i >= j, return 0 (single char or empty is already a palindrome).
If s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j), return dfs(i + 1, j - 1).
Otherwise, return 1 + min(dfs(i + 1, j), dfs(i, j - 1)).

optimal.idea: Interval dynamic programming computing the minimum insertion cost for substrings of increasing length in O(n^2) time and O(n) space.
steps: Let dp[j] store the minimum insertions for substring s[i..j].
Iterate i from n-1 down to 0, maintaining a prevDiag variable to hold dp[j-1] before update.
For j from i+1 to n-1: if s[i] == s[j], dp[j] = prevDiag; else dp[j] = 1 + min(dp[j], dp[j-1]).
prevDiag is updated with old dp[j].
Return dp[n-1].

whyNext: Builds on common subsequence construction from Longest Common Subsequence (Seq 261) by using the LCS DP table to reconstruct the minimal merged sequence that includes both strings as subsequences.
hints: Compute the standard 2D LCS table dp[i][j] for str1 and str2.
Backtrack from (len(str1), len(str2)) towards (0, 0): when characters match (str1[i-1] == str2[j-1]), emit that character once and move diagonally.
When characters differ, emit the character corresponding to the larger dp direction (up or left) and decrement that index.

brute.idea: Recursive backtracking exploring all possible interleaved supersequence characters until both strings are consumed.
steps: Recursive dfs(i, j):
If i == len(str1), return str2[j..end].
If j == len(str2), return str1[i..end].
If str1[i] == str2[j], return str1[i] + dfs(i+1, j+1).
Else branch: cand1 = str1[i] + dfs(i+1, j), cand2 = str2[j] + dfs(i, j+1).
Return shorter of cand1 and cand2.

optimal.idea: Compute 2D LCS table in O(n * m) time, then trace back from (n, m) to build the shortest supersequence in O(n + m) time.
steps: Compute dp[n+1][m+1] where dp[i][j] is the length of LCS of str1[0..i) and str2[0..j).
Initialize pointers i = n, j = m and StringBuilder res.
While i > 0 and j > 0: if str1[i-1] == str2[j-1], append str1[i-1] and decrement both i and j; else if dp[i-1][j] >= dp[i][j-1], append str1[i-1] and i--; else append str2[j-1] and j--.
Append remaining characters from str1 or str2.
Reverse res and return string.

whyNext: Builds on interval game theory from Shortest Common Supersequence (Seq 494) context by formulating minimax decisions where each player chooses an outer pile to maximize their net stone differential.
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the maximum relative score difference (current player - opponent) on piles[i..j].
Current player can pick piles[i] (yielding piles[i] - dp[i+1][j]) or piles[j] (yielding piles[j] - dp[i][j-1]).
Because the total number of piles is even and sum is odd, Alice can always pick all odd-indexed or all even-indexed piles, guaranteeing a win.

brute.idea: Minimax DFS exploring picking from left vs right end recursively to check if player 1 can achieve a strictly positive score advantage.
steps: Recursive minimax(i, j):
If i == j, return piles[i].
Return max(piles[i] - minimax(i + 1, j), piles[j] - minimax(i, j - 1)).
Return true if minimax(0, n-1) > 0.

optimal.idea: Interval dynamic programming calculating max differential across all subarray intervals in O(n^2) time and O(n) space.
steps: Initialize dp array of size n with dp[i] = piles[i].
For interval length len from 2 to n: for left index i from 0 to n - len: j = i + len - 1.
dp[i] = max(piles[i] - dp[i + 1], piles[j] - dp[i]).
Return dp[0] > 0 (mathematically always true for Alice under the game constraints).

whyNext: Builds on game theory minimax DP from Stone Game (Seq 495) by generalizing to any array length and non-odd total sums where ties are allowed and Player 1 wins if final differential >= 0.
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the maximum score margin the current player can achieve from nums[i..j].
Player chooses nums[i] or nums[j]: dp[i][j] = max(nums[i] - dp[i+1][j], nums[j] - dp[i][j-1]).
If the final score margin for the whole array dp[0][n-1] >= 0, Player 1 can win or tie.

brute.idea: Recursively evaluate all combinations of choices by both players using pure minimax.
steps: Recursive minimax(i, j):
If i == j, return nums[i].
Return max(nums[i] - minimax(i + 1, j), nums[j] - minimax(i, j - 1)).
Return minimax(0, n - 1) >= 0.

optimal.idea: Interval dynamic programming optimized to a 1D array representing score differences in O(n^2) time and O(n) space.
steps: Initialize dp array of size n with dp[i] = nums[i].
For length from 2 to n: for i from 0 to n - length: j = i + length - 1.
dp[i] = max(nums[i] - dp[i + 1], nums[j] - dp[i]).
Return dp[0] >= 0.

whyNext: Builds on minimax game choices from Predict the Winner (Seq 496) by allowing a variable number of piles X (1 <= X <= 2M) to be taken from the start, updating M = max(M, X) dynamically.
hints: Let dp(i, M) be the maximum stones the current player can take from suffix piles[i..n-1] with parameter M.
If 2M >= n - i, the player can take all remaining piles: sum(piles[i..n-1]).
Otherwise: player tries taking X piles for 1 <= X <= 2M, leaving opponent with dp(i + X, max(M, X)). The player gets suffixSum[i] - dp(i + X, max(M, X)).

brute.idea: Recursively try every valid pile count X from 1 to 2M, computing opponent's optimal response.
steps: Precompute suffix sums of piles.
Recursive dfs(i, M):
If i + 2*M >= n, return suffixSum[i].
Try every X in [1, 2*M]: take suffixSum[i] - dfs(i + X, max(M, X)).
Return maximum stones found.

optimal.idea: Memoized 2D dynamic programming storing max stones for state (index i, parameter M) in O(n^3) time.
steps: Precalculate suffixSum array where suffixSum[i] is sum of piles[i..n-1].
Initialize memo table memo[n][n+1] with 0.
For state (i, M): if i + 2*M >= n, return suffixSum[i].
Iterate X from 1 to 2*M: best = max(best, suffixSum[i] - dfs(i + X, max(M, X))).
Memoize and return memo[i][M].

whyNext: Builds on minimax state search from Stone Game II (Seq 497) by modeling an adversarial guessing scenario where we minimize the worst-case total cost to guarantee guessing a number in range [1..n].
hints: Let dp(i, j) be the minimum cost to guarantee finding the target number in range [i..j].
Base case: if i >= j, cost is 0 (0 or 1 candidate remaining means no wrong guess penalty).
For a guess k in [i..j], worst-case penalty is k + max(dp(i, k-1), dp(k+1, j)). Minimize this worst-case over all possible k.

brute.idea: Recursively explore picking every number k in [i..j] as the first guess, taking the worst branch and minimizing over k.
steps: Recursive dfs(i, j):
If i >= j, return 0.
Set minCost = infinity.
For k from i to j: cost = k + max(dfs(i, k - 1), dfs(k + 1, j)); minCost = min(minCost, cost).
Return minCost.

optimal.idea: Interval dynamic programming building min-max costs for increasing range lengths in O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space.
steps: Initialize dp table of size (n+2) x (n+2) with 0.
Iterate interval length len from 2 to n.
For start i from 1 to n - len + 1: end j = i + len - 1.
dp[i][j] = min over k in [i, j] of (k + max(dp[i][k-1], dp[k+1][j])).
Return dp[1][n].

whyNext: Builds on interval partition DP from Matrix Chain Multiplication / Burst Balloons (Seq 273) by choosing split points k that minimize the non-leaf node sum while tracking the max leaf in each partition.
hints: Every non-leaf node equals the product of the largest leaf in its left subtree and the largest leaf in its right subtree.
Partitioning arr[i..j] into arr[i..k] and arr[k+1..j] contributes max(arr[i..k]) * max(arr[k+1..j]) plus the subproblem costs.
Can also be solved greedily in O(n) using a monotonic decreasing stack, always multiplying the smallest available leaf by the smaller of its adjacent neighbors.

brute.idea: Recursively try every split index k in [i, j-1] to partition the interval into left and right subtrees.
steps: Recursive dfs(i, j):
If i == j, return 0 (leaves contribute 0 to the sum of non-leaf nodes).
For each split k from i to j-1: cost = max(arr[i..k]) * max(arr[k+1..j]) + dfs(i, k) + dfs(k+1, j).
Return minimum cost across all split points.

optimal.idea: Monotonic decreasing stack greedily pairing smaller adjacent leaves with the minimum of their neighbors in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize stack with Integer.MAX_VALUE.
For each value x in arr: while stack.peek() <= x: pop mid = stack.pop(); add mid * min(stack.peek(), x) to total.
Push x onto stack.
While stack.size() > 2: pop mid = stack.pop(); add mid * stack.peek() to total.
Return total sum.

whyNext: Builds on interval DP from Matrix Chain Multiplication / Burst Balloons (Seq 273) by sorting cut points, adding stick boundaries 0 and n, and choosing the optimal first cut k in range (i, j) that incurs cost (cuts[j] - cuts[i]).
hints: Add boundaries 0 and n to the cuts array and sort it ascending.
Let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost to make all cuts between index i and index j.
Base case: if j == i + 1, no cuts remain between them, cost = 0. Otherwise, for every k between i and j: cost = (cuts[j] - cuts[i]) + dp[i][k] + dp[k][j].

brute.idea: Recursively attempt every available cut within the current stick segment, paying the current segment length each time.
steps: Augment cuts array with endpoints 0 and n, then sort.
Recursive dfs(i, j):
If j <= i + 1, return 0 (no cuts to make).
For each k from i + 1 to j - 1: cost = (cuts[j] - cuts[i]) + dfs(i, k) + dfs(k, j).
Return min cost across all cuts k.

optimal.idea: Interval dynamic programming calculating minimum cutting cost for segments of increasing length in O(m^3) time and O(m^2) space.
steps: Create array all of length m + 2 with 0, cuts, and n, then sort ascending.
Initialize dp table of size (m+2) x (m+2).
Iterate interval difference diff from 2 to m + 1: for left index i from 0 to m + 1 - diff: j = i + diff.
dp[i][j] = (cuts[j] - cuts[i]) + min_{k in (i, j)}(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]).
Return dp[0][m + 1].
